lently, as by a blow or strain; part by a rupture of substance; fracture: used primarily of rigid solid materials: as, to ''break'' a stone or a stick; to ''break'' a wall.
{{smaller block|<poem>And the widows of Ashur are loud in their wail,
And the idols are ''broke'' in the temple of Baal.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Destruction of Sennacherib.}}}}
'''2.''' Specifically, in ''law'', to open or force one’s way into (a dwelling, store, etc.) burglariously.
{{smaller block|A house is said to be ''broken'' by a burglar when any part or fastening of it is removed with intent to effect an entrance.}}
'''3.''' To destroy the continuity of in any way; destroy the order or formation of; disconnect; interrupt; disorder; specifically, of the skin, lacerate: as, to ''break'' the center of an army; to ''break'' ranks; the stone, falling, ''broke'' the surface of the water; to ''break'' an electric circuit; to ''break'' one’s sleep; the blow ''broke'' the skin.
{{smaller block|This hereditary right should be kept so sacred as never to ''break'' the succession. ''Swift'', Sent. of Ch. of Eng. Man, ii.
<poem>No other object ''breaks''
The waste, but one dwarf tree.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Julian and Maddalo.}}}}
'''4.''' To destroy the completeness of; remove a part from; hence, to exchange for a smaller amount, as a bank-note in payment: as, to ''break'' a set of chessmen; to ''break'' a ten-dollar bill.
{{smaller block|But I am uneasy about these same four guineas: I think you should have given them back again to your master; and yet I have ''broken'' them. ''Richardson'', Pamela, xvii.}}
'''5.''' To lessen, impair, or destroy the force, strength, or intensity of; weaken: as, a constitution ''broken'' by dissipation; to ''break'' a child’s will; to ''break'' the force of a blow.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|break|669|break}}</noinclude>lently, as by a blow or strain; part by a rupture of substance; fracture: used primarily of rigid solid materials: as, to ''break'' a stone or a stick; to ''break'' a wall.
{{smaller block|<poem>And the widows of Ashur are loud in their wail,
And the idols are ''broke'' in the temple of Baal.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Destruction of Sennacherib.}}}}
'''2.''' Specifically, in ''law'', to open or force one’s way into (a dwelling, store, etc.) burglariously.
{{smaller block|A house is said to be ''broken'' by a burglar when any part or fastening of it is removed with intent to effect an entrance.}}
'''3.''' To destroy the continuity of in any way; destroy the order or formation of; disconnect; interrupt; disorder; specifically, of the skin, lacerate: as, to ''break'' the center of an army; to ''break'' ranks; the stone, falling, ''broke'' the surface of the water; to ''break'' an electric circuit; to ''break'' one’s sleep; the blow ''broke'' the skin.
{{smaller block|This hereditary right should be kept so sacred as never to ''break'' the succession. ''Swift'', Sent. of Ch. of Eng. Man, ii.
<poem>No other object ''breaks''
The waste, but one dwarf tree.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Julian and Maddalo.}}}}
'''4.''' To destroy the completeness of; remove a part from; hence, to exchange for a smaller amount, as a bank-note in payment: as, to ''break'' a set of chessmen; to ''break'' a ten-dollar bill.
{{smaller block|But I am uneasy about these same four guineas: I think you should have given them back again to your master; and yet I have ''broken'' them.
{{right|''Richardson'', Pamela, xvii.}}}}
'''5.''' To lessen, impair, or destroy the force, strength, or intensity of; weaken: as, a constitution ''broken'' by dissipation; to ''break'' a child’s will; to ''break'' the force of a blow. {{smaller block|An old man, ''broken'' with the storms of state.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iv. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|I’ll rather leap down first and ''break'' your fall.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Too courteous are you, fair Lord Lancelot.
I pray you, use some rough discourtesy
To blunt or ''break'' her passion.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''6.''' To tame; train to obedience; make tractable: as, to ''break'' a horse or a hunting-dog for work in the field.

{{smaller block|Why, then thou canst not ''break'' her to the lute?
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1.}}}}
'''7.''' To violate, as a contract, law, or promise, either by a positive act contrary to the law or promise, or by neglect or non-fulfilment.

{{smaller block|<poem>Unhappy man! to ''break'' the pious laws
Of nature.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''8.''' To make bankrupt, as a bank or a merchant; destroy, as the credit of a bank.

{{smaller block|The credit of this bank being thus ''broken'' did exceedingly discontent the people.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 12, 1672.}}}}
'''9.''' To reduce in or dismiss from rank or position as a punishment: as, to ''break'' an officer.

{{smaller block|It must be allowed, indeed, that to ''break'' an English freeborn officer only for blasphemy was, to speak the gentlest of such an action, a very high strain of absolute power.
{{right|''Swift'', Against Abolishing Christianity.}}}}

{{smaller block|The captain . . . has the power to turn his officers off duty, and even to ''break'' them and make them do duty as sailors in the forecastle.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 11.}}}}
'''10†.''' To disband.

{{smaller block|My birthday was ominous. . . . The regiment in which my father served being ''broke.''
{{right|''Sterne.''}}}}
'''11.''' To make a first and partial disclosure of, as an opinion or project; especially, to impart or tell cautiously so as not to startle or shock; also, simply, tell; inform: as, to ''break'' unwelcome news to a person.
{{smaller block|His nerves are so weak, that the sight of a poor relation may be too much for him. I should have gone first to ''break'' it to him.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, v. 1.}}}}
'''12†.''' To cut up, as game. {{smaller|Skill in breaking the killed deer was considered as important in venery as boldness in the chase itself.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They found him by a water side,
Where he ''brake'' the beast that tide,
The hart that was so wild.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Triamour'', in Ellis Collection.}}}}
'''13.''' To tear. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|In this county [Hampshire] ''break'' is used for tear, and tear for ''break:'' as, I have a-torn my best decanter or china dish; I have ''a-broke'' my fine cambric apron.
{{right|''Grose.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''To break a blockade''', to render it inoperative by driving off or destroying the blockading force.—'''To break a gun''', to open it by the action.—'''To break a jest''', to utter a jest; crack a joke.   ''Otway; Bolingbroke.''—'''To break a lance''', to enter the lists with an opponent; make a trial of skill.—'''To break an electrical circuit.''' See ''circuit.''—'''To break a path, a road,''' or '''a way''', to force a passage through obstacles or difficulties.—'''To break bread.''' (''a'') To take a meal; share one’s hospitality. (''b'') To celebrate the communion.—'''To break bulk.''' (''a'') To begin to unload. (''b'') To remove a part from a parcel or quantity of goods.}}
{{smaller block|I heard S<sup>r</sup> R. Howard impeach S<sup>r</sup> W<sup>m</sup> Pen in the House of Lords, for ''breaking bulk'' and taking away rich goods out of the E. India prizes formerly taken by Lord Sandwich.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, April 9, 1668.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To break camp,''' to pack up tents and camp-utensils, and resume the march.—'''To break cover''' or '''covert,''' to come forth from a lurking-place or concealment, as game when hunted.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>On this little knoll, if anywhere,
There is good chance that we shall hear the hounds:
Here often they ''break covert'' at our feet.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To break down.''' (''a'') To take down by breaking; destroy by breaking: as, to ''break down'' a fence: figuratively, to overcome: as, to ''break down'' all opposition. (''b'') To pass (the press-cake of gunpowder) between the toothed rollers of a granulating machine.—'''To break gates.''' See ''gate''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To break ground.''' (''a'') To upturn the surface of the ground; dig; plow. (''b'') To dig; open trenches; commence excavation, as for building, siege operations, and the like; hence, figuratively, to begin to execute any plan.}}
{{smaller block|How happy, could I but, in any measure, . . . make manifest to you the meanings of Heroism; the divine relation . . . which in all times unites a Great Man to other men; and thus, as it were, not exhaust my subject, but so much as ''break ground'' on it.
{{right|''Carlyle'', Heroes and Hero-Worship, i.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'')   ''Naut.'', to release the anchor from the bottom.—'''To break in,''' to tame; discipline; make tractable, as a horse.—'''To break jail''' or '''prison,''' to make one’s escape from confinement.—'''To break joint,''' to be so arranged, as stones, bricks, shingles, etc., in building, that the joints in one course do not coincide with those in the contiguous courses. See ''bond''<sup>1</sup>.}}
{{smaller block|A wire cable is composed of many threads, and these completely ''break joint'' with each other, and thus neutralize any defect in the wires. {{right|''Luce'', Seamanship, p. 241.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To break liberty''' or '''leave''' (''naut.''), to remain away from a ship after the time specified for returning.—'''To break squares.''' See ''square''.—'''To break of a habit''' or '''practice,''' to cause to abandon it.—'''To break off.''' (''a'') To sever by breaking: as, to ''break off'' a twig. (''b'') To put a sudden stop to; interrupt; discontinue; leave off; give up: as, to ''break off'' a marriage engagement.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All amazed ''brake off'' his late intent.</poem> {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 469.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She ended here, or vehement despair
''Broke off'' the rest. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 1008.}}</poem>}}

'''To break one’s fast''', to take the first food of the day. See ''breakfast''.
{{smaller block|Happy were our forefathers, who ''broke their fasts'' with herbs. {{right|''Taylor.''}}}}

'''To break one’s head''', to cut one’s head by a blow; stun or kill one by a blow upon the head.
{{smaller block|He has ''broke my head'' across, and has given Sir Toby a bloody coxcomb too. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1.}}}}

'''To break one’s heart''', to become heart-broken or grievously afflicted: as, he ''broke his heart'' over her misfortunes.—'''To break one’s mind''', to reveal one’s thoughts: with ''to''.
{{smaller block|''Break thy mind'' to me. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I, who much desir’d to know
Of whence she was, yet fearful how to ''break''
''My mind'', adventur’d humbly thus to speak. {{right|''Dryden.''}}</poem>}}

'''To break one’s word''', to violate a promise or pledge; act contrary to an engagement.—'''To break open''', to force open; unclose by violence: as, to ''break open'' a door.—'''To break out a cargo''', to unstow it so that it may be easily unloaded.—'''To break Priscian’s head''', to violate the rules of grammar. [Priscian was a celebrated Roman grammarian.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Fair cousin, for thy glances,
Instead of ''breaking Priscian’s head''
I had been breaking lances. {{right|''Praed.''}}</poem>}}

'''To break ranks''' (''milit.''), to leave the ranks; fall out.—'''To break step''' (''milit.''), to cease marching in cadence; march at will.—'''To break the back''', to strain or dislocate the vertebræ as with too heavy a burden.—'''To break the back of.''' (''a'') To destroy the force or efficiency of; weaken at a vital point: as, one mistake ''broke the back of'' the enterprise. (''b'') ''Naut.'', to break the keel and keelson of, as a ship. (''c'') Figuratively, to accomplish the greater or most difficult part of: as, to ''break the back of'' a heavy piece of business.—'''To break the bank.''' See ''bank''<sup>2</sup>.—

'''To break the grain''', to destroy a tendency to crystallize, as in stearic acid by mixture with palmitic acid.—'''To break the heart of''', to afflict grievously; cause great sorrow or grief to; cause to die of grief.—'''To break the heartstrings of''', to inflict great grief or hopeless sorrow upon; afflict overwhelmingly.
{{smaller block|No time to break jests when ''the heartstrings'' are about to be ''broken''.
{{right|''Fuller'', Jesting.}}}}
'''To break the ice''', to overcome obstacles and make a beginning; especially, to overcome the feeling of restraint incident to a new acquaintanceship.
{{smaller block|I have often formed a resolution to ''break the ice'', and rattle away at any rate.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''ice'' of ceremony being once ''broken''.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}
'''To break the neck''', to dislocate a joint of the neck.—'''To break the neck of.''' (''a'') To destroy the main force of; ruin or destroy.
{{smaller block|''Breaks the neck of'' their own cause.
{{right|''Milton.''}}}}
(''b'') To get over the worst part of; get more than half through.
{{smaller block|He was a capital spinner of a yarn when he had ''broken the neck of'' his day’s work.
{{right|''Hughes.''}}}}
'''To break the parle†''', to begin the parley.   ''Shak.''—'''To break up.''' (''a'') To cut up, as game.
{{smaller block|<poem>Boyet, you can carve;
''Break up'' this capon.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iv. 1.}}}}
(''b'') To open or lay open: as, to ''break up'' a floor; to ''break up'' fallow ground. (''c'') To discontinue or put an end to: as, to ''break up'' housekeeping. (''d'') To separate; disintegrate; disband: as, to ''break up'' a company or an army. (''e'') To impair; exhaust; fatigue greatly.
{{smaller block|The six hours of deadly terror which I then endured have ''broken'' me ''up'' body and soul.
{{right|''Poe'', Tales, I. 161.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To break upon the wheel,''' to torture or put to death by stretching on a cart-wheel, or a wooden frame in the form of a St. Andrew’s cross, and breaking the limbs with an iron bar: a mode of punishment formerly much used in some parts of Europe.—'''To break water,''' to rise to the surface of the water, as a fish.}}
{{smaller block|Numbers of these fish [bluefish] may be seen ''breaking water'' at any time on the banks and shoals.
{{right|''Sportsman’s Gazetteer'', p. 258.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To break wind,''' to give vent to wind from the body by the anus.—'''To break word†''', to violate a pledge or an obligation.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They that ''break word'' with Heaven will break again
With all the world, and so dost thou with me.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iii. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be separated into parts or fragments under the action of some force, as a blow or a strain; become fractured: as, the rock ''broke'' into a thousand pieces; the ice ''broke'' under his feet.—'''2.''' To become discontinuous, disconnected, disordered, or disintegrated; lose continuity or formation: as, at the last charge the line ''broke''; the circuit ''broke''.
{{smaller block|The command, Charge, was given, and was executed with loud cheers and with a run; when the last of the enemy ''broke''. {{right|''U. S. Grant'', Personal Memoirs, I. 351.}}}}
'''3.''' Specifically—(''a'') To change suddenly and involuntarily from a natural to a higher and shriller tone or to a whisper: said of the voice. (''b'') In ''music'': (1) To change from one register to another, as a musical instrument. (2) To change from one combination of pipes to another, especially when having more than one pipe to the note: said of compound organ-stops, like the mixture, the cornet, etc.—'''4.''' To change from one gait into another: said of a horse: as, to ''break'' into a gallop.—'''5.''' To burst; happen or begin to be with suddenness or violence.
{{smaller|(''a'') To discharge itself spontaneously, as a tumor.}}
{{smaller block|The same old sore ''breaks'' out from age to age.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Walking to the Mail.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To burst forth or begin with violence, as a storm.}}
{{smaller block|A second deluge o’er our heads may ''break''. ''Dryden.''

The whole storm, which had long been gathering, now ''broke'' at once on the head of Clive.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Clive.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') To burst into speech or action: generally followed by ''out''. (See phrases below.)}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I would not have your women hear me
''Break'' into commendation of you; ’tis not seemly.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') To begin as if with a burst or break.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And from our own the glad shout ''breaks'',
Of Freedom and Fraternity! ''Whittier'', Pæan.</poem>}}

'''6.''' To become impaired, weakened, or reduced; especially, to decline in health, strength, or personal appearance.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’m sorry Mopsa ''breaks'' so fast:
I said her face would never last.</poem>
{{right|''Swift'', Cadenus and Vanessa.}}}}

'''7.''' To begin to be: said specifically of the day, dawn, or morning.
{{smaller block|Is not that the morning which ''breaks'' yonder?
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The day of wrath, against which Leibnitz had warned the monarchs of Europe, was beginning to ''break''.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. Const., II. 365.}}}}

'''8.''' To force one’s way (into, out of, or through something).
{{smaller block|Go, ''break'' among the press, and find a way out To let the troop pass fairly.{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., v. 3.}}}}
'''9.''' To fail in trade or other occupation; become bankrupt.
{{smaller block|He that puts all upon adventures doth oftentimes ''break'' and come to poverty.{{right|''Bacon'', Riches.}}}}
{{smaller block|There came divers of Antonio’s creditors in my company to Venice, that swear he cannot choose but ''break.''{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The true original chairs were all sold, when the Huntingdons ''broke.''{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 217.}}}}
'''10.''' To lose friendship; become hostile; be in opposition or antagonism: commonly with ''with.''
{{smaller block|To ''break'' upon the score of danger or expense is to be mean and narrow-spirited.{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Friendship.}}}}
'''11.''' In ''pool'', to make a break; make the first shot or opening play. See ''break'', ''n.'', 15.—'''12.''' ''Naut.'', to hog or sag.—'''13.''' In ''hort.'': (''a'') To put forth new buds. (''b'') To flower before the proper time.
{{smaller block|In our turnip and carrot-beds a few plants often ''break'' —that is, flower too soon.{{right|''Darwin'', Var. of Animals and Plants, p. 5.}}}}
'''14†.''' To broach a subject; come to an explanation: with ''to'' or ''with.''
{{smaller block|The chamber beeing voyded, he ''brake with'' him in these tearmes.{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues and his England, p. 227.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then, after, ''to'' her father will I ''break.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, i. 1.}}}}

'''To break across.''' {{smaller|See ''across.''}}—'''To break away.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To disengage one’s self abruptly; escape, as from a captor, by sudden and violent action; hence, to leave suddenly.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Fear me not, man, I will not ''break away.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iv. 4.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
